## Statement

Let $P$ be countably generated, $\phi$-irreducible and aperiodic with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose $D$ is petite with probability $\nu$ and multiplier $\alpha>0$, and $C\subseteq D$ is $(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small for this same $\nu$, with $\nu(C)>0$ and $\nu\ll\pi$. Then $D$ is small at some common time.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The kernel, irreducibility, aperiodicity, invariant probability, petite inequality on $D$, and same-measure small-set minorization on $C$.

[F1] [[def-petite-set-for-markov-kernel]]: $\sum_{n\ge1}a_nP^n(x,\cdot)\ge\alpha\nu(\cdot)$ on $D$.

[F2] [[def-small-set-minorization-and-drift]]: $P^m(y,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu$ on $C$.

[F3] [[lem-aperiodic-minorization-times-are-cofinite]]: once every state can reach a minorization into $\nu\ll\pi$, $\nu P^n\ge c_n\nu$ for every sufficiently large $n$.

[F4] [[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]: every positive-$\phi$ set is accessible from every state.

[F5] [[thm-discrete-strong-markov-property]]: the chain restarts from its state at the first entrance time.

[F6] [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]: $\pi P^n=\pi$ for every $n\ge0$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: the canonical path/stopping-time construction uses AC as specified by [F5].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and facts [F1]–[F5], with [A1].

1.1 The petite inequality on $C$ gives $\sum_na_nP^n(x,C)\ge\alpha\nu(C)>0$ for every $x\in D$. Choose $M$ so $\sum_{n>M}a_n<\alpha\nu(C)/2$. Since $P^n(x,C)\le\Pr_x(\tau_C\le n)\le\Pr_x(\tau_C\le M)$ for $n\le M$, the truncated weighted sum gives $\Pr_x(\tau_C\le M)\ge q:=\alpha\nu(C)/2$ uniformly on $D$. [F1, given]

1.2 Since $\nu(C)>0$ and $\nu\ll\pi$, $\pi(C)>0$. To see that every state has positive probability of reaching $C$, let $H=\{x\in C^c:P^n(x,C)=0\text{ for every }n\ge1\}$. Kernel iteration makes $H$ measurable. If $x\in H$ and $P(x,H^c)>0$, the countable union $H^c=C\cup\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{y:P^n(y,C)>0\}$ has a member of positive $P(x,\cdot)$-mass; integrating the corresponding positive function gives $P^{n+1}(x,C)>0$, a contradiction. Thus $P(x,H)=1$ for every $x\in H$. Irreducibility then forces $\phi(H^c)=0$, since no point of $H$ can reach $H^c$; hence $\phi(H)>0$. For every $n\ge1$, invariance and $P^n(x,H)=1$ on $H$ give $\int_{H^c}P^n(x,H)\,\pi(dx)=0$. Irreducibility says every $x\in H^c$ has $P^n(x,H)>0$ for some $n$, so the countable union of these $\pi$-null level sets is $H^c$ and $\pi(H^c)=0$, contradicting $\pi(C)>0$. Therefore $H=\varnothing$. For every state choose $n(x)\ge1$ with $P^{n(x)}(x,C)>0$; then $P^{n(x)+m}(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon P^{n(x)}(x,C)\nu(\cdot)$. By [F3], $\nu P^t\ge c_t\nu$ for every $t\ge N_0$. Choose $L>M+m+N_0$. For every $0\le s\le M$ and $y\in C$, $P^{L-s}(y,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu P^{L-s-m}(\cdot)\ge\epsilon c_{L-s-m}\nu(\cdot).$ The minimum $c>0$ over these finitely many $s$ is positive. [F2, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1]

2.1 Decompose at the first hitting time $\tau_C=s\le M$. The strong Markov property and step 1.2 give $P^L(x,\cdot)\ge c\nu(\cdot)\Pr_x(\tau_C\le M)\ge cq\nu(\cdot)$ for every $x\in D$. This is one fixed-time minorization, so $D$ is small. [F5, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\pi$ be invariant for $P$, and suppose $PV\le\lambda V+b1_C$ with $V\ge1$, $0<\lambda<1$, and $\sup_CV<\infty$. Then $\pi V<\infty$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The invariant probability and drift inequality in the Statement.

The supremum is interpreted in the extended reals, with $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$; the empty-set case is handled separately below.

[F1] [[def-small-set-minorization-and-drift]]: $V$ is finite-valued and $PV\le\lambda V+b1_C$ pointwise.

[F2] [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]: $\pi P=\pi$, including equality of integrals for bounded measurable functions.

[F3] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: $P(V\wedge N)$ is measurable and bounded by $N$.

[F4] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: $\int(V\wedge N)d\pi\uparrow\int Vd\pi$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and facts [F1]–[F4].

1.1 If $C=\varnothing$, then $PV\le\lambda V$ everywhere. For each integer $N\ge1$, $V_N=V\wedge N$ satisfies $PV_N-V_N\le-(1-\lambda)V$ on $\{V\le N\}$ and $PV_N-V_N\le0$ on $\{V>N\}$. Invariance for the bounded function $V_N$ gives integral zero, so $\pi(\{V\le N\})=0$. Since $V$ is finite-valued, these sets increase to the whole space, contradicting that $\pi$ is a probability. Thus no invariant probability exists in the empty-set case, and the implication is vacuous. Assume $C\ne\varnothing$ below. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 Set $V_N=V\wedge N$. Since $V_N\le V$ and $V_N\le N$, $PV_N\le \min(PV,N)$. On $C$, $PV_N-V_N\le\lambda\sup_CV+b$. On $C^c\cap\{V\le N\}$ it is at most $-(1-\lambda)V$, and on $C^c\cap\{V>N\}$ it is at most zero. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Invariance for bounded $V_N$ gives $\int(PV_N-V_N)d\pi=0$. Using the three pointwise bounds from step 1.2, $(1-\lambda)\int_{C^c\cap\{V\le N\}}V\,d\pi\le(\lambda\sup_CV+b)\pi(C)\le\lambda\sup_CV+b.$ [F2, step 1.2]

2.2 The domains $C^c\cap\{V\le N\}$ increase to $C^c$; monotone convergence bounds $\int_{C^c}Vd\pi$ by the right side divided by $1-\lambda$. The integral over $C$ is at most $\sup_CV$. Hence $\pi V<\infty$. [F4, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\phi$ be a finite nonzero measure on a countably generated measurable space. For measurable $A,B\subseteq\mathsf X^2$, define $E=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in A,\ (y,z)\in B\}$. If $\phi^{\otimes3}(E)>0$, then there are measurable $C,D$ with $\phi(C),\phi(D)>0$ and $\gamma>0$ such that
$$\phi(A_1(x)\cap B_2(z))\ge\gamma\quad(x\in C,\ z\in D),$$
where $A_1(x)=\{y:(x,y)\in A\}$ and $B_2(z)=\{y:(y,z)\in B\}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite measure, countably generated sigma-algebra, and product-measurable sets in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-measurable-space]]: countable generation supplies increasing finite partitions generating the product sigma-algebra.

[F2] [[lem-finite-measure-sets-are-approximable-by-a-generating-algebra]]: under a finite measure every measurable set has arbitrarily close symmetric-difference approximants in a generating algebra.

[F3] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: product integrals equal iterated section integrals.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and facts [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Put $\eta=\phi^{\otimes3}(E)>0$. The product measure is finite because $\phi$ is finite. By [F1], the union of the algebras of increasing finite tensor-product partitions is an algebra generating the product sigma-algebra. Apply [F2] to obtain a member $H$ of that algebra with $\phi^{\otimes3}(E\mathbin\triangle H)<\eta/6$. Then $\phi^{\otimes3}(H)>5\eta/6$ and $\phi^{\otimes3}(H\setminus E)<\eta/6<\phi^{\otimes3}(H)/4$, so $E$ occupies more than three quarters of $H$. The set $H$ is a finite union of tensor cells at a common partition level. If every positive-measure cell had occupancy at most three quarters, finite additivity would give the same upper bound on $H$, a contradiction. Thus some cell $U\times V\times W$ has positive product measure and $\phi^{\otimes3}(E\cap(U\times V\times W))>\tfrac34\phi(U)\phi(V)\phi(W)>0$. Only one finite-algebra approximant and one cell of its finite partition are selected; no conditional-expectation representative or choice axiom is used. [F1, F2, F3, given, choose, algebra]

1.2 Since $E\subseteq A\times_{\!y}B$, Tonelli gives $\int_{U\times V}1_A(x,y)\,d\phi(x)d\phi(y)>\tfrac34\phi(U)\phi(V),$ and likewise $\int_{V\times W}1_B(y,z)\,d\phi(y)d\phi(z)>\tfrac34\phi(V)\phi(W)$. Consequently the sets $C=\{x\in U:\phi(A_1(x)\cap V)>\tfrac34\phi(V)\}$ and $D=\{z\in W:\phi(B_2(z)\cap V)>\tfrac34\phi(V)\}$ have positive measure; otherwise the corresponding integral could not exceed three quarters of the rectangle measure. [F3, step 1.1]

2.1 For $x\in C$ and $z\in D$, both sections occupy more than three quarters of $V$. The complement of their intersection in $V$ is the union of two sets, each of measure less than $\phi(V)/4$. Thus $\phi(A_1(x)\cap B_2(z))\ge\phi(V)/2>0$. Set $\gamma=\phi(V)/2$. [step 1.2, algebra] ∎
